story: On August 15, 1977, the Big Ear radio telescope in Ohio picked up a startlingly powerful, 72-second radio blast from deep space. Operating as part of the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence, or SETI, the telescope detected a narrowband signal at 1420 megahertz, a frequency matching the natural emission line of neutral hydrogen. Astronomer Jerry Ehman discovered the anomaly a few days later while reviewing computer printouts. Stunned by its intensity—thirty times higher than the surrounding background noise—he circled the reading '6EQUJ5' and scrawled 'Wow!' in the margin. Despite decades of follow-up searches, the signal has never repeated. While some scientists suspected extraterrestrial life, and others suggested terrestrial interference or comets, recent studies propose it may have been caused by a rare astrophysical phenomenon: a magnetar flare energizing a cold hydrogen cloud.
angle: A mysterious 72-second radio blast from the constellation Sagittarius was so intense and precisely matched the hydrogen frequency that an astronomer instinctively wrote 'Wow!' on the printout, sparking a decades-long alien mystery.

claims.claim: The Wow! signal was detected on August 15, 1977.
The signal was detected by Ohio State University's Big Ear radio telescope.
Astronomer Jerry R. Ehman discovered the anomaly while reviewing computer printout data.
Ehman circled the intensity reading '6EQUJ5' and wrote 'Wow!' beside it.
The entire signal sequence lasted for the full 72-second observation window of the telescope.
The signal appeared to come from the direction of the constellation Sagittarius.
The signal's frequency was around 1420 megahertz, which matches the natural emission line of neutral hydrogen.
The Big Ear telescope was dismantled in 1998.
Despite numerous follow-up searches over the decades, the signal has never recurred.
Antonio Paris proposed that hydrogen clouds surrounding comets like 266P/Christensen could be the source.
The comet hypothesis was dismissed by astronomers because the comets were not in the beam at the correct time.
A 2024 study suggested the signal could have been caused by a rare astrophysical event where a magnetar flare energized a cold hydrogen cloud.

disputed: Whether the signal was caused by extraterrestrial intelligence, terrestrial radio interference, a passing comet, or a magnetar-energized hydrogen cloud; scripts should attribute specific theories to researchers or present them as hypotheses.
